title: What really happens when you crack your knuckles

post.youtube_title: What Actually Happens When You Crack Your Knuckles? #shorts
post.caption: It's not your bones. In 2015, scientists filmed it inside an MRI. And one doctor cracked only ONE hand for 60+ years to test the arthritis myth 🤯
post.pinned_comment: How many times a day do you crack yours? 👇

sources: Kawchuk et al. (2015), 'Real-Time Visualization of Joint Cavitation', PLOS ONE
Unger (1998), 'Does knuckle cracking lead to arthritis of the fingers?', Arthritis & Rheumatism; 2009 Ig Nobel Prize in Medicine
deWeber et al. (2011), J Am Board Fam Med: no link between knuckle cracking and hand osteoarthritis

beats.text: That *pop* when you crack your knuckles? It isn't your bones breaking.
And it isn't your joints grinding together, either.
Every knuckle is a joint wrapped in a tiny *capsule*, filled with a slippery liquid called *synovial* *fluid*.

beats.text: When you stretch or bend your finger, the space inside the joint gets *bigger*, and the pressure drops.

beats.text: For decades, scientists *argued* about what happens next.
So in {2015|twenty fifteen}, researchers in Canada filmed knuckles cracking inside an *MRI* scanner.
At the exact moment of the *pop*, they saw a gas *bubble* suddenly form inside the fluid.

beats.text: That's also why you can't crack the same knuckle twice in a row. It takes about *twenty* minutes for the gas to dissolve back in.
But does cracking them give you *arthritis*?
One doctor, Donald Unger, tested it on himself.
For more than *sixty* years, he cracked the knuckles on his left hand, but never on his right.
In the end, *neither* hand had arthritis. And in {2009|two thousand nine}, he won an *Ig* *Nobel* Prize for it.
Bigger studies agree. There's *no* good evidence it causes arthritis.
So, how many times a day do you crack yours?
